say.text: A 46-year-old man has a fatty liver on ultrasound, and the same scan shows a 2 cm gallstone. He has never had pain, jaundice or fever.
What is your plan for the stone?

choices.label: No treatment for now; he returns if colic, jaundice or fever begins
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy now, since stones can lead to cholecystitis and cancer
Ursodeoxycholic acid for six months to dissolve the stone early
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. About 80 per cent of gallstones never cause symptoms, and a silent stone turns symptomatic only about 1 to 2 per cent a year.
Surgery is kept for symptoms or a specific high-risk feature, and this man has neither.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Not right. Stones look like a hidden time bomb, so removing one now feels like prevention.
But a silent stone turns symptomatic only about 1 to 2 per cent a year, so most operations would treat people who would never have had trouble.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: a stone is an indication only when it causes symptoms or carries a specific high risk.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Not right. Tablets feel like a gentle way to clear stones without an operation.
But ursodeoxycholic acid dissolves only small radiolucent cholesterol stones in a functioning gallbladder, and stones often recur after it is stopped.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: check the stone type and the gallbladder before any tablet.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Ask first what this stone has done to him so far. Then ask what would make a stone worth acting on.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: A 55-year-old man has recurrent colic. Plain X-ray shows several small, radio-opaque stones, and his gallbladder contracts normally.
He asks whether tablets can dissolve them. What do you advise?

choices.label: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy; tablets will not clear radio-opaque stones
Ursodeoxycholic acid for 6 to 12 months, since the stones are small
Ursodeoxycholic acid now, with surgery only if colic returns

say.text: Yes. Symptomatic stones need removal, and these are the kind tablets cannot dissolve.
Dissolution is for small radiolucent cholesterol stones in a functioning gallbladder; anything else needs the operation.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Not right. Six months of a cheap drug feels sensible when the stones are small.
But size is not the qualifier that matters; the drug works only on radiolucent cholesterol stones, and a radio-opaque stone is not dissolved by it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the stone type is the qualifier here, not the size.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Not right. Trying tablets first feels cautious, and surgery can always wait for a relapse.
But the tablets do not work on this stone, and stones often recur after stopping them, so the colic keeps coming back.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: symptoms are the reason to act, not a reason to delay.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: A 38-year-old man on a ventilator after a road traffic injury and laparotomy has fever and right upper pain.
Ultrasound shows a distended, thick-walled gallbladder with no stone. He is too unstable for an operation today. What is the treatment of choice now?

choices.label: Percutaneous cholecystostomy to drain the gallbladder until he is fit for surgery
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy in this admission, as the definitive treatment
Immediate open cholecystectomy, since open surgery is the safest option when unwell
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Acalculous cholecystitis in a critically ill patient comes from stasis and ischaemia, so the gallbladder is fragile.
Drainage is the option this patient can tolerate, and it buys time until he is fit.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Not right. With no stone to deal with, a single operation can look like the simple, complete answer.
But he cannot yet tolerate a general anaesthetic and pneumoperitoneum, so fitness decides what the operation can be.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: check first whether the patient can survive the operation.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Not right. Acute cholecystitis is usually operated early, and open surgery feels like the surest way to finish the job.
But early surgery is reserved for fit patients, and this man is too unstable for any operation today.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the grade and the fitness of the patient come before the choice of operation.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Ask what this patient can tolerate today, and what the gallbladder needs over the next few days.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Now the reason. Why does drainage beat an operation for this gallbladder?

choices.label: Fragile from stasis and ischaemia, so drainage eases it without operative stress
Drainage cures the inflammation, so the gallbladder never needs an operation
Without a stone it is milder and can safely wait

say.text: Yes. Without a stone the gallbladder still becomes ischaemic, and gangrene and perforation are more common than in calculous disease.
Drainage relieves the gallbladder safely for now, and the definitive operation comes when the patient can take it.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Not right. Drainage does relieve the gallbladder quickly, so it can feel like a complete cure.
But drainage is a bridge for patients too ill for surgery, and it does not settle every later decision.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Not right. No stone means no blockage, so the gallbladder seems to have less reason to be dangerous.
But acalculous disease runs a worse course, with more gangrene, perforation and mortality than the calculous form.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Two structures enter the gallbladder during laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and the duct looks clear enough to clip.
Before you clip, what must come first?

choices.label: Clear the triangle, separate the lower gallbladder, then confirm the view
Nothing more: two structures entering the gallbladder complete the view
Clip the cystic duct as soon as it enters the gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The view needs three things: a cleared triangle, a separated lower gallbladder, and two and only two structures seen.
Two structures alone is not enough; they count only once the triangle and the cystic plate are clear.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Not right. The two structures are the most memorable part of the view, so they can feel like the whole test.
But they count only once the triangle is cleared and the lower gallbladder is off the liver bed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the view is three requirements, not one.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Not right. The duct is the structure you must not cut, so clipping it early feels careful.
But you can identify it safely only after the triangle is clear, so the view comes before any clip.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: identification comes from clearing the field, not from spotting the duct first.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Think about what must be cleared before any structure is divided, and where the gallbladder still touches the liver.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: What is the commonest cause of a major bile duct injury during laparoscopic cholecystectomy?

choices.label: Misidentifying the common bile duct as the cystic duct, then dividing it
Bleeding from the cystic artery, clipped blindly across the field
Injury to the right hepatic artery during dissection of the triangle

say.text: Yes. Most major duct injuries come from mistaken anatomy, not bleeding, which is why the view comes before the clip.

choices.label: Next

say.text: Not right. Bleeding is the dramatic event surgeons fear most, so it can feel like the usual cause.
But the usual route to a major duct injury is a mistake about which duct is which, not a bleed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: ask which error is commonest, not which is most feared.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Not right. The hepatic artery lies close to the triangle, so injury there feels like the main vascular risk.
But the commonest major duct injury is an identification error at the duct, and vascular injury is less common.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: it is the duct that is misread, not the artery.

choices.label: Try again
